parts.label: (a)
parts.part_stem:
Two long straight wires P and Q are parallel to each other, as shown in Fig. 8.1. There is a current in each wire in the direction shown.

The pattern of the magnetic field lines in a plane normal to wire P due to the current in the wire is also shown.

{{figure:figure_8_1}}

Fig. 8.1

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Draw arrows on the magnetic field lines in Fig. 8.1 around wire P to show the direction of the field.

markscheme_points.text: at least one anticlockwise arrow and no clockwise arrows drawn on field lines

hints: Hint 1: Picture gripping wire P with your right thumb pointing along the current (upwards) and think which way your fingers naturally curl around the wire when viewed from above.
parts.proper_answer: Arrows drawn anticlockwise on all field circles when viewed from above.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the right-hand grip rule**
Imagine holding wire P with your right hand with your thumb pointing up along the current. Your curled fingers show the sense of the $B$-field circles.

Step 2: **Apply to the view from above**
With current coming up out of the plane toward you, the fingers curl anticlockwise. So draw a small arrowhead on each circle pointing anticlockwise, all in the same sense.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the direction of the force on wire Q due to the magnetic field from wire P.

markscheme_points.text: force on wire Q is directed to the left (towards wire P)

hints: Hint 1: Focus on wire Q: its current is upwards, and the $B$-field from wire P at the position of Q is at right angles to the line joining P to Q - think what Fleming's left hand gives for the force direction.
parts.proper_answer: Force on wire Q is directed towards wire P, to the left.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the field from P at Q**
The concentric circles from P reach Q. For an anticlockwise pattern, the field line at Q points perpendicular to the P-Q line. Combined with the upward current in Q, Fleming's left hand gives a force sideways.

Step 2: **Remember the parallel-current rule**
Two wires carrying current in the same direction attract each other. So the $B$-field of P pulls Q back toward P, i.e. to the left.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text:
The current in wire Q is less than the current in wire P.

State and explain whether the magnitude of the force on wire P is less than, equal to, or greater than the magnitude of the force on wire Q.

markscheme_points.text: Newton's third law of motion (action-reaction pair) or force depends on product of currents

hints: Hint 1: Think beyond $F = BIL$ for one wire alone - the two wires exert forces on each other as a pair of interacting bodies.
Hint 2: Recall what Newton's third law says about the magnitudes of two forces when body A pushes on body B and B pushes back on A, even if currents and fields are different.
parts.proper_answer: Equal to. The forces on P and Q form a Newton third law action-reaction pair, so magnitudes are equal and directions opposite, independent of the different currents.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See the two forces as a pair**
Wire P creates a $B$-field that acts on Q, and wire Q creates a $B$-field that acts on P. Although $B$ at each wire is different because $I_P \ne I_Q$, each force is $F = BIL$ for that location.

Step 2: **Apply Newton's third law**
Whenever Q pushes on P magnetically, P pushes back on Q with equal magnitude and opposite direction: $$F_P = F_Q$$ So the magnitude on P is equal to the magnitude on Q.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
Nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (NMRI) is used to obtain diagnostic information about internal structures in the human body.

Radio waves are produced and directed towards the body. The radio waves affect the protons within the body.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Explain why radio waves are used.

markscheme_points.text: frequency of radio waves is e

hints: Hint 1: Think about what protons do in the strong uniform magnetic field of the NMRI scanner before any radio waves arrive - they precess at a particular frequency.
Hint 2: Think about the condition for a proton to absorb energy efficiently from an electromagnetic wave and jump to the higher energy spin state.
parts.proper_answer: The frequency of the radio waves equals the precession (Larmor) frequency of the protons, so resonance occurs and protons absorb energy and are excited to the higher energy state.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Protons precess in the main field**
In NMRI a large uniform $B$-field makes hydrogen protons precess like tiny tops at the Larmor frequency, with two closely spaced energy states (spin up and spin down).

Step 2: **Match frequencies for resonance**
The energy gap $\Delta E = hf$ corresponds to a radio frequency photon. When the applied radio waves have frequency $f$ equal to the precession frequency, resonance occurs and protons strongly absorb the radio energy and flip to the excited state.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Explain why the radio waves are applied in pulses.

markscheme_points.text: Any 1 from: • protons de-excite • protons emit r.f. pulses • emitted (r.f.) pulse (from

hints: Hint 1: Think about when the detector could hear a tiny signal from the body if the powerful transmitting radio pulse were left on continuously.
Hint 2: Think about what excited protons do as soon as the exciting pulse switches off and what signal that process produces.
parts.proper_answer: Radio waves are pulsed so detection occurs in between pulses when the transmitter is off. Excited protons de-excite and emit r.f. pulses which are detected and used to form the image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Need a quiet time to listen**
While the large transmitted pulse is on, it would swamp any tiny signal from the body. Switching it off leaves a quiet interval in between pulses for measurement.

Step 2: **Detect the relaxation emission**
In that interval the excited protons relax back to the lower state, emitting radio-frequency radiation. This emitted r.f. is picked up by coils and its strength and decay time give information about the tissue type and proton density.
